#5289. Beyond commission splits: How wellness benefits give brokerages a recruiting edge

Brokerages are expanding benefits aimed at agent well-being, from access to group-style PPO options to coaching on stress and resilience. Executives frame the programs as foundational support as market conditions remain uncertain heading into 2027.  AI Summary

By many estimations, real estate professionals are facing the most challenging housing market in recent memory in 2027. Unlike in the past, many will be doing so with access to more resources than ever designed to ensure they are feeling healthy, at the peak of their game and ready to tackle whatever the 2027 housing market throws at them.

This is because over the past year, several brokerages announced a variety of wellness programs and health insurance opportunities they are now offering to agents, who as independent contractors, typically do not have access to things like insurance through their brokerage.

Since the start of 2026, ENRG Realty, Compass International Holdings, Equity Union Real Estate and John R. Wood Properties have announced the launch of health insurance or wellness benefits initiatives.

“We were founded on Maslow Hierarchy of Needs, so health insurance fits right in with some of the core basic values that we need to provide to our agents so they can be successful and thrive,” Erinn Nobel, the co-founder and president of ENRG Realty and a HousingWire Woman of Influence award winner, said. “In order for our agents to function at a high level, they can’t be sitting at home worried about an illness or being able to pay their bills because they don’t have health coverage. It is a foundational offering and a benefit for us to be able to provide it for our agents.”

Nobel said that while some Realtor boards or associations offer health insurance, there is often just one policy option, something she experienced first hand after moving to Alaska from Washington state.

“It was great to be able to access insurance through our board, but there was only one plan, so you couldn’t shop around,” Nobel said. “It just didn’t sit well with me that my options were so limited.”

A similar experience with challenges accessing insurance for his family is also what inspired Harma Hartouni, the CEO of Equity Union Real Estate, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, to begin providing his agents with access to group-style health coverage options, including a nationwide PPO network, through a partnership with Trident BPO.

When he approached the executive team about launching this initiative, Hartouni said they were a bit divided as to whether or not they should do this.

“Some thought the agents wouldn’t care, but some of our managers thought it was great,” Hartouni said. “Ultimately, our agents are our clients, and I knew that if these people were not healthy or not in a clear mindset in this challenging market, they would not function well.”

In the current uncertain economic environment, Hartouni added that the offering has also provided many agents, who previously had access to insurance through a spouse who lost their job, a level of peace of mind that they couldn’t previously provide.

“The consistent feedback from agents is that they are saving money and are able to see better doctors,” Hartouni said.

Nobel said she’s heard similar feedback from her agents. After rolling out the program, Nobel said she and her team received countless messages from agents saying thank you. Beyond better serving existing agents, Nobel said the program also helped ENRG Realty with agent recruitment.

“It has become an attraction magnet for us. Savvy agents that have been in the industry for a while are starting to really compare brokerages and look at what benefits they get from each brokerage and the different values they provide,” Nobel said. “If an agent already has access to health insurance through a spouse or partner, then this may not convey the same value as it would to a self-employed single mom who would love to have access to health care.”

Hartouni has also noticed the agent recruitment benefits of offering health insurance.

“The smart broker is looking for producing agents that are in the middle of their career, where they still have plenty of years left in the business to learn and grow, but have already begun to establish themselves,” he said. “But these agents often have families to think about and how can we help them have one less thing to worry about? We can provide them with access to health insurance.”

While John R. Wood Properties is not providing agents with access to health insurance, the brokerage recently announced it was providing its agents with access to individualized coaching focused on their personal well-being and professional development, through a partnership with HatchPath. Through the program, agents can gain access to coaching support across a wide range of areas including nutrition, stress management, mental resilience, leadership, career development and major life transitions.

“People are just so burn[ed] out in general and everybody is on edge from personal challenges, financial challenges, family challenges. I just thought what better way to support our people than to give them access to coaching,” Corey McCloskey, the president of John R. Wood Properties, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, said. “I think a lot of us who run businesses have realized that you bring your whole self to work. You can’t just turn off what’s happening in your personal life when you walk into your office — it affects you whether you realize it or not.”

While still in the early stages of the rollout, McCloskey said she has seen her agents and staff use HatchPath coaching for help with everything from financial planning to fitness and overall physical wellness.

Although brokerages are continuing to face challenging housing market conditions and ever-tightening profit margins, these executives believe it’s important for brokerages to support their agents beyond just professional development.

“If we are encouraging people to be entrepreneurs, we have to support them and provide them some sort of value,” Nobel said. “Anytime we can offer a benefit that has real value to agents, we really look to do that because ultimately that is what we as a brokerage are supposed to do — provide value for our agents.”

Nobel added that she would encourage more brokerages to consider providing agents with access to health insurance.

“This is something that we need to be offering our agents in the world right now,” she said. “Offering insurance is what is best for our industry.”

McCloskey, a HousingWire Woman of Influence, shares a similar view.

“Knowing that not only us, but other companies are supporting agents as whole people, I think that will only serve to make our industry better,” she said. “The younger leaders coming into the industry have seen the toll this industry can take on someone who doesn’t take care of themselves. They want to do things differently, and I think we have an opportunity now that we’ve never had before where we can offer these sorts of things to people and really tell them how important they are to us.”

#5288. Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

#5287. TRADOC's Final Commander, Gen. Gary Brito (Ret.), Joins Qtonic Quantum Ahead of CNSA 2.0 Deadline

Leading the Army Readiness Council, Brito brings 38 years of Army training and readiness leadership as national security systems move to post-quantum cryptography

MIAMI, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Gen. Gary M. Brito, U.S. Army (Ret.), the 18th and final commanding general of U.S. Army Training and Doctrine Command (TRADOC), has joined Qtonic Quantum to lead the Army Readiness Council and serve as Senior Military Advisor to the Founders. His appointment comes 39 days before NSA's CNSA 2.0 compliance date for new national security system acquisitions.

Under CNSSP 15 and NSA's CNSA 2.0 guidance, all new national security system acquisitions are required to be CNSA 2.0 compliant, meaning quantum-resistant, by Jan. 1, 2027. NIST finalized its first post-quantum cryptography standards, FIPS 203, 204 and 205, in August 2024. Adversaries can harvest encrypted data today and decrypt it once quantum computers mature.

Brito retired as a four-star general after a 38-year Army career. At TRADOC he led the command responsible for the Army's institutional training, education and leader development. He also led the strategy, planning and early integration of TRADOC's merger with Army Futures Command, which culminated in the activation of the new U.S. Army Transformation and Training Command in October 2025. He previously commanded the Maneuver Center of Excellence and Fort Benning and the Joint Readiness Training Center and Fort Polk, served as the Army's 49th Deputy Chief of Staff, G-1, the Army's senior human resources officer, and deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan.

As leader of the Army Readiness Council, Brito will drive the council's work on how post-quantum migration is planned and measured as a readiness problem across Army and joint environments. He will also advise the founders on how Qtonic Quantum serves defense and government leaders. He serves in a personal capacity, and his views do not represent the Department of the Army or the Department of War. He joins a team that includes senior retired military leaders.

"Readiness is built, not declared," said Lt. Gen. (Ret.) Roger L. Cloutier Jr., former commander of NATO Allied Land Command and Founding Chair of the Allied Defense Council at Qtonic Quantum. "General Brito spent 38 years building it at the scale of an institution. Post-quantum migration is a readiness problem, and he will help us put evidence in front of the leaders who set the schedule."

"Leaders at all levels are charged to ensure unit readiness against all threats," said Brito. "Communications and data readiness is no different. Leaders need to inventory what they depend on, test it and fix it on a schedule they set, not one an adversary sets."

Qtonic Quantum's Find. Prove. Fix. approach starts with QScout Gold, which delivers quantum cyber risk and vulnerability intelligence, a crypto-agility assessment and a signed cryptographic bill of materials (CBOM). Together they give leaders an evidence-backed inventory of the cryptography their systems depend on.

Brito holds a bachelor's degree from Penn State University, where the Penn State Alumni Association named him a 2025 Alumni Fellow, and a master's degree in human resource management from Troy University.

Qtonic Quantum Corp. provides quantum cyber risk and vulnerability intelligence for enterprise and federal environments. Its Find. Prove. Fix. approach connects risk intelligence, adversarial validation and migration advisory to help organizations prioritize action and prepare for post-quantum security. #5286. CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler in record-setting $43.9B cybersecurity deal

CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. today announced plans to acquire Zscaler Inc., a fellow provider of cybersecurity software, for about $43.9 billion.

The all-stock deal values the latter company at $260.40 per share. That’s a 34% premium to Zscaler’s closing price on Friday, the day CrowdStrike’s takeover interest became public. The transaction would be the largest cybersecurity acquisition on record by a wide margin.

Investors weren’t entirely thrilled. CrowdStrike’s shares fell 9% today, an indication that might think it’s an awfully large pill to swallow. Zscaler’s stock, however, rose almost 18%.

The companies reported their quarterly results in conjunction with the acquisition announcement. Both topped expectations across the board. CrowdStrike posted adjusted net income of $354.9 million on $1.58 billion in revenue, while Zscaler reported a $208.4 million adjusted profit and sales of $949.3 million. The former company also boosted its full-year guidance.

CrowdStrike’s flagship Falcon platform uses lightweight programs called sensors to protect employee devices, cloud instances and other technology assets. Zscaler’s Zero Trust Exchange, in turn, protects the network connections that link together those assets. The platform is positioned as an alternative to virtual private network tools.

The Zero Trust Exchange encrypts the traffic that flows between employee devices and business applications. When needed, administrators can decrypt the data to search for threats. Additionally, they can configure the platform to require more thorough authentication when users log into particularly sensitive systems.

The product portfolios of CrowdStrike’s and Zscaler overlap in some areas. Both companies offer tools that can protect artificial intelligence applications from threats such as prompt injections. They also compete in the secure browser category, although their respective offerings take different approaches to blocking malware.

Zscaler offers a tool that can automatically launch simulated cyberattacks against applications to find weak points. CrowdStrike joined the fray as well earlier this year with SafeMind, a set of custom AI models and related assets. It not only finds software vulnerabilities but also develops detections, automated workflows designed to spot hacking attempts.

CrowdStrike said that it will use the network telemetry collected by Zscaler to enhance SafeMind’s training dataset. In 2024, the latter company disclosed that its platform blocked more than 9 billion threats per day. That activity, which has no doubt grown in volume since, should give CrowdStrike’s AI models a more complete understanding of hacker behavior.

The company’s plans for Zscaler also extend beyond AI training. CrowdStrike will incorporate the network protection provider’s software into its Flex offering, which enables customers to buy multiple cybersecurity tools via a single contract. That could help expand the adoption of Zscaler’s products among CrowdStrike customers.

The companies have also identified other upselling opportunities. They disclosed today that about 8,000 Zscaler customers don’t yet use CrowdStrike products.

“With Zscaler, we’re building cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely,” said CrowdStrike founder and Chief Executive Officer George Kurtz (pictured). “We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen.”

CrowdStrike expects to complete the acquisition in the second half of its 2028 fiscal year, which starts next February. The company stated that the deal will be “significantly and immediately accretive” to free cash flow per share upon closing.

CrowdStrike expects Zscaler’s financial impact to grow over time. It estimates that the deal will unlock $500 million worth of annual cost synergies within 18 to 24 months, mainly in the form of data center, supplier and operational improvements. The company also sees Zscaler boosting its annual revenue run-rate by $1 billion within 30 months.

#5285. Cost cutting is not cost reduction; builders and trades face a test

Strategem estimates tariffs add $12,919 to a typical new home, while NAHB data shows combined construction inputs up 10.4% year over year. Builders are seeking concessions, but long-run savings may require operational fixes with trade partners.  AI Summary

A reliable estimate of the tariff burden on a typical newly built American home puts the cost at $12,919, or about $4.88 per square foot.

That is before accounting for broader inflation in construction labor, transportation, services and other inputs that homebuilders must absorb while trying to make their homes affordable to increasingly price-sensitive customers.

This informed baseline calculation of tariff impact at the new-home level, developed by homebuilding supply-chain consultancy Strategem through its Strategy Pulse Pro platform, updates the National Association of Home Builders‘ April 2025 builder-reported tariff-cost estimate of $10,900 to reflect subsequent trade-policy changes. The model distributes tariff exposure across 17 material categories, with hardware and fasteners, steel products, lumber, cabinets, windows and aluminum accounting for some of the highest estimated costs.

By its nature, Strategem’s tally is a modeled cost burden, not a direct measure of tariffs paid on every home or of the amount passed through to buyers.

Still, it illustrates a difficult dilemma for homebuilders, and one none of them can simply avoid: Costs imposed upstream cannot necessarily be recovered downstream. And in that downstream market, households increasingly lack the financial capacity or confidence to buy homes at the prices builders need to charge.

That predicament, predictable in a falling market, is a reflexive homebuilding firm response that reverberates through homebuilding’s wider ecosystem like a bad-trip flashback. Homebuilders are looking to their suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, and trade contractors to shoulder more of the financial pain.

It’s a law of dismal science physics during a downturn: Wringing a bit of margin improvement by most builders means squeezing suppliers’ margins into further negative territory.

The danger is that some builders may, and often do, push their business partners beyond what they can reasonably absorb. This tactic, seductive as it may seem as a way to claw back input cost reductions, mostly serves as a temporary fix. Ultimately, such quick fixes undermine the very production capacity, service reliability, and competitive supplier pools they will need to survive the downturn and recover.

Homebuilders have spent much of the past two years using price reductions, mortgage-rate buydowns and other incentives to preserve sales velocity. Those concessions have helped sustain production, but they have also eroded the earnings cushion – the “shock absorber” – that previously allowed many builders to absorb rising costs without substantially disrupting operations.

The squeeze is occurring on both sides of builders’ income statements. According to NAHB’s November 13 analysis of Producer Price Index data, goods used in new residential construction rose 9.8% year over year in October, while service inputs increased 11.3%. The combined input index rose 10.4%, including a 5.8% increase in building-material prices.

These are input-price indexes, not equivalent percentage increases in the total cost of constructing a house. Still, they reveal why slowing demand has not delivered the broad-based cost relief builders might otherwise expect.

The pressure is particularly difficult for smaller builders and suppliers with limited financial reserves. They must keep enough business flowing to cover fixed costs while protecting the margins and working capital required to remain viable.

Ken Pinto, a longtime homebuilding strategic-sourcing executive and co-founder of Strategem, and a friend of The Builder’s Daily, believes the industry risks conflating two fundamentally different types of cost reduction.

Purchasing departments are reporting savings from increasingly competitive bidding, he says, but those reductions often come from suppliers sacrificing profitability rather than from lasting improvements in how homes are built.

“When you reduce costs by going out to bid, going out to bid, going out to bid, you’re not taking cost out of the supply chain; you’re taking margins out,” Pinto says.

This self-preservatory instinct among homebuilding business decision-makers has important, potentially risky, consequences. A trade contractor who accepts a lower price to keep crews working may provide immediate relief to a builder’s direct costs, but the underlying costs of labor, transportation, insurance, equipment, and materials may remain unchanged.

When demand eventually recovers, those concessions may disappear. More troubling, some suppliers may not survive long enough to participate in the recovery.

Pinto points to manufacturers facing higher costs for steel, copper and resin-based products while struggling to secure corresponding price increases. Their customers may be able to delay accepting price increases, but the underlying costs do not disappear simply because builders refuse to pay them. The resulting margin compression can become unsustainable.

Conversations with homebuilding purchasing professionals suggest that the opportunities for further reductions vary considerably by category. Some material suppliers remain willing to compete aggressively for market share, particularly in areas where slower construction activity has created excess capacity. But trade contractors face different circumstances.

Years of declining production volume have already weakened some local subcontractor businesses. In some markets, established trade firms have closed, while others struggle with cash flow, payment disputes and mechanics’ liens.

At the same time, immigration enforcement has reduced labor availability in trades including framing, concrete, masonry, roofing, electrical work and painting. The result is an increasingly uneven marketplace in which a builder may find materials readily available but struggle to secure the skilled labor required to install them.

Residential construction also faces growing competition for certain resources from the extraordinary investment flowing into artificial intelligence infrastructure and data-center construction.

That competition is particularly acute in markets where large commercial projects – especially of note in Texas and Virginia ­– require concrete, electrical equipment, transportation capacity and specialized labor. Although residential and data-center construction workforces are not interchangeable, competition for certain services and materials can raise costs even as homebuilding activity slows.

The risk extends into 2027. A contractor with too little work today may be unable to retain skilled crews until demand improves. A builder who pushes that contractor’s prices below sustainable levels may find the contractor has disappeared, downsized, or committed its remaining capacity elsewhere when new-home orders return.

That is not merely a supplier problem. It becomes a builder’s problem across the construction cycle, quality, customer service, and profitability.

Pinto argues that builders and trade contractors have a much larger opportunity to improve profitability by jointly addressing avoidable operating costs.

One recurring example is construction scheduling. When a subcontractor arrives at a jobsite that is not ready, the contractor incurs labor, transportation and administrative costs without productive work. Unreliable schedules make it harder to allocate crews, while late changes, rework and unnecessary return visits consume resources neither party can afford to waste.

“We still get subcontractors showing up to job sites, and the job’s not ready for them. So, a dry run. This shouldn’t be happening,” Pinto says.

Consider the contrasting approach between 1. a homebuilder demanding a 5% reduction in a trade contractor’s bid and 2. the two businesses collaborating to eliminate repeated crew mobilizations, incomplete jobsite preparation and avoidable rework.

The first approach may reduce the builder’s invoice while leaving the contractor’s expenses unchanged. The second can reduce the actual cost of completing the work, creating room for both companies to improve their economics.

Achieving these operational efficiencies becomes especially important when homebuilding’s lower production volumes should give operating teams more opportunity to coordinate schedules, standardize specifications and eliminate recurring inefficiencies.

Pinto is developing a collaborative workshop, Tearing Down the Walls, with former subcontractor and Builderbeast Consulting founder Don Bronchick and industry colleague Andrew Stevens. The workshop’s premise is that builders and trade contractors can improve their economics by jointly examining the processes that create unnecessary costs.

The approach requires both parties to share information, acknowledge their contributions to inefficiency, and agree on measurable improvements. That is more demanding than threatening to award a contract to the lowest bidder, but it offers the possibility of savings that endure through a market recovery.

Homebuilding’s consolidation wave adds another dimension to the challenge. Larger builders have gained substantial purchasing leverage, but their long-term returns increasingly depend on integrating local operating expertise, supplier relationships and construction capabilities to build more effective enterprises.

The purchasing organization offering the lowest quoted prices does not necessarily lead to the lowest completed-home costs. A supplier who consistently meets schedules, maintains qualified crews, resolves field problems quickly, and supports a builder through fluctuations in demand may be worth more than the nominal difference between competing bids.

That does not excuse poor performance or prevent builders from replacing suppliers who cannot meet reasonable cost, quality, or service requirements. Competitive bidding remains necessary, and some vendors may still have room to lower their prices.

The key question is whether builders understand and choose between extracting a concession and improving the economics of the entire production process.

For 2027, the choice to improve holistic economics should guide purchasing and operating decisions. Builders need to understand which costs suppliers can control, which are driven by external forces, and which stem from the builder’s own practices. They also need to evaluate suppliers’ financial health, preserve alternative sources of capacity where practical, and measure total installed costs rather than purchase prices alone.

These measures will not close the affordability gap or restore lost homebuyer demand. Nor can they fully offset tariffs, higher financing costs, or skilled-worker shortages. They can, however, prevent homebuilders from worsening their operating position while trying to protect near-term margins.

Homebuilding companies have every reason to ask their business partners to share the burden of a difficult market. But there is a meaningful difference between sharing that burden and transferring it to a partner with no capacity to absorb it. Business leaders know the difference.

They know the ones best positioned for recovery may not be those that extract the deepest concessions today. They know that the real, more structural solution – and one that should keep most valued partner relationships intact – reduces the actual cost of producing homes while preserving the trust and transparency, skills and productive capacity that will allow them to build profitably when customers return.

That’s not to say it’s the easier, softer way forward, but when demand finally strengthens, a homebuilder will need more than an order backlog and available lots. That team will need capable partners still willing – and able – to build the homes. And they know it.

#5284. Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious plan to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

“I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he said. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

#5282. So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in new hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one company.

“It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.”

Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual company. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.

Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue quickly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

One venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

1) Think VERY big, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a company that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

There are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Big Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a company of their own or a year with their family.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

Learn more about the technology making it all work.

#5281. Raleigh’s housing reforms helped ease rents, Pew study finds

Pew reports Raleigh’s post COVID zoning reforms helped add 16,884 homes from 2021 to 2024. The city’s supply growth coincided with slower rent gains and a 15% inflation adjusted rent decline from 2022 to 2025.  AI Summary

For years, homebuilding leaders have argued that the most effective way to lower housing costs is to build more, and that cities that adopt pro-housing reforms will be rewarded with greater supply and more attainable housing. New research from The Pew Charitable Trusts shows what happened when Raleigh, N.C., followed that playbook.

Following the pandemic, Raleigh overhauled its zoning and land use laws to make building easier, Pew found. The result was a building boom, particularly for the townhomes and apartments the city’s earlier rules constrained. This uptick in homebuilding made renting more affordable in North Carolina’s capital city, especially for middle-income households and younger residents.

The report highlights how adding new housing supply at scale can improve housing affordability, echoing similar impacts that followed concerted rezoning efforts in Minneapolis-St. Paul, Minn., and Austin, Texas. The same dynamic is playing out across the Sun Belt, where many of the nation’s fastest-growing metros also have some of the loosest zoning rules, and where rents and home prices have dropped more dramatically than anywhere else in the country.

Raleigh didn’t rely on a single fix to make building housing easier. Its reforms combined a rewrite of its form-based code, an end to parking minimums, denser building near transit and a housing bond to support affordable housing.

“Of all of the drivers of housing costs – population growth, an influx of high-income earners, high land costs and high construction costs – we have the most agency and direct control over restrictive zoning regulations,” Patrick Young, Raleigh’s planning and development director, said in a statement.

Raleigh’s 2021 zoning reform, which expanded the city’s already-established form-based code, opened the door to more “missing middle” housing. It did so by replacing units-per-acre caps with physical standards such as lot size, yards, and building height.

The changes legalized duplexes, triplexes and quadplexes in more residential districts and expanded where townhomes can be built. Under the new form-based code, further refined in 2022, builders can now construct small apartment buildings and tiny houses with up to two dwelling units on compact infill lots.

As a result, builders can now construct missing middle housing in more of Raleigh’s neighborhoods, a shift that Pew links to better affordability for middle-income and younger residents.

Raleigh eliminated its citywide parking minimums in 2022. That allowed developers to fit more housing units on each property and, in some cases, spared them the expense of building costly parking structures, which can often make a project too costly to pursue.

The city also spurred housing growth by allowing taller, denser buildings near major transit corridors. Transit Overlay District zones allowed for an extra story along Bus Rapid Transit corridors, extending half a mile along some local bus routes.

Additionally, a density bonus allows developers to exceed height limits by up to 50% if at least 20% of the extra units are designated as affordable, below-market units.

The City of Raleigh approved an $80 million housing bond in 2020 that is projected to create at least 700 affordable homes, fund homebuyer assistance and help homeowners with home repairs.

About $14 million has already gone to four developments totaling more than 240 units, while another $24 million in gap financing will back over 470 additional units, more than 90% of which will be affordable to households earning 60% of area median income or less.

Between 2021 and 2024, Raleigh added 16,884 housing units, growing its housing stock by 7.7%, even as the city’s population grew by 5.8% over the same period. Raleigh’s housing growth also outpaced the state (5.7%) and national (3.2%) rates during that period.

Of the 16,884 units added, roughly 2,000, or 12%, were affordable to households earning 80% or less of area median income (AMI), with Raleigh’s housing bond funds helping support their development. Density bonuses contributed about 200 of those affordable units, accounting for 10% of the total.

Additionally, Raleigh’s code changes intentionally shifted a large share of production away from detached single-family homes toward townhomes, duplexes and tiny homes. Since 2021, the city has issued more than twice as many townhouse permits as in 2015 to 2020, and has permitted more than 200 duplex units and over 200 accessory dwelling units (ADUs).

As a result, average monthly rents rose at only half the national pace and fell in real, inflation-adjusted terms. Pew’s analysis estimates inflation-adjusted rents declined 15% from 2022 to 2025, and, as of 2025, the income needed to afford the city’s median rent dropped from 79% of AMI to 65%.

Raleigh’s experience mirrors a wider trend among fast-growing Sun Belt markets, where less restrictive zoning and fewer barriers to housing development have supported greater housing production and helped moderate housing costs. The South accounted for more than half of all U.S. housing starts between 2021 and 2025, while Sun Belt markets continue to lead the nation in rent and home price declines.

According to Yardi Matrix’s October 2026 multifamily report, rents fell year over year in 12 major US markets. The Sun Belt accounted for ten of those, led by Austin, Houston, Nashville, Tampa and Phoenix. The for-sale market shows a similar pattern, with home prices dropping disproportionately in the Sun Belt while climbing in the Northeast and Midwest.

#5280. Cisco and OpenAI Launch Shirudo, A New Project to Safeguard Agentic AI

An industry-first open source project, Shirudo, helps systems defend themselves at machine speed

SAN JOSE, Calif., Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) and OpenAI today launched an open source effort to make infrastructure secure by default and able to defend itself against today's sophisticated cyber attacks. For too long, security has been a coat of paint. Cisco builds protection into the infrastructure itself, drawing on decades of building and protecting the systems the world depends on. OpenAI brings leading frontier AI research and insight into the attacks coming next. Together, they combine their insight to help anticipate AI-driven threats with the control to stop them.

Defenders must protect every part of their infrastructure, all the time. Attackers only need one machine that hasn't been patched. Shirudo is an important step toward closing that gap. The goal is infrastructure that is hardened from the moment it is built, keeps getting harder to attack, and can be restored to a known-good state if it is compromised.

"There is nothing more important than giving security teams the tools they need to match the speed of the AI-driven threats they are facing. We need self-defending infrastructure that acts at the speed of code, learns in real time, and shields itself until patches are safely rolled out," said Jeetu Patel, Cisco President and Chief Product Officer. "Today, we're proud to announce Shirudo with OpenAI, an important step towards that vision as we continue to collaborate with the wider community to solve the unique challenges of AI safety and security."

"We're giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn't mean you can patch every system tomorrow," said Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI. "We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Now when one team finds a better way to protect a system, others don't have to start from scratch."

Shirudo: An Open Source Project from Cisco and OpenAIShirudo, Japanese for "shield," uses eBPF, a technology that runs small, custom programs inside the operating system kernel without changing its source code. With it, AI agents can find a vulnerability, build a shield, and test that it stops the attack without disrupting the service. Shields go live only when the evidence says they are safe. Every shield is cryptographically signed, so the host can verify it before it runs, even if an attacker has gained administrator access.

In testing against recent critical vulnerabilities "Java4shell" and the PHP flaw, Shirudo was able to write code that detected and blocked attempts to exploit both threats. By utilizing an agentic framework, Shirudo matches the speed of AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified. Learn more about Shirudo here.

Cisco and OpenAI are inviting developers, researchers, and enterprises to help shape what comes next. Contribute a test that reproduces a vulnerability, run a shield against a kernel build you use, or show us where it breaks legitimate traffic. To learn more about Shirudo, visit: https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo.

#5279. Matters.AI raises $12M as it expands its data security business in North America

Enterprise data security startup Matters.AI today announced that it has raised $12 million in new funding as it expands its business in North America.

Matters.AI offers a platform called the AI Security Engineer for Data that is designed to protect sensitive data used by employees, artificial intelligence systems and AI agents across the enterprise. Formerly known as OptiQ.AI, the company has teams in the San Francisco Bay Area and Bengaluru, India.

AI agents, the company argues, now have the same access to enterprise data as the employees who run them. Visibility into who or what is using that data is missing from most data security tools, according to Matters.AI, leaving security teams to connect alerts from separate tools by hand.

Security teams using Matters.AI get one place to see where sensitive data resides, where it has traveled and who or what has accessed it. Data is tracked across cloud environments, on-premises systems, software-as-a-service applications, endpoints and browsers. The company’s AI analyzes the context of that data and the intent behind each use.

Underneath that view, sensitive data across the data estate is discovered and classified, according to the company. Matters.AI also uses patented fingerprinting, built on large language models, to follow data as it moves between systems.

Insider risk and compliance risk are identified by correlating four signals, those being data sensitivity, misconfiguration, access and intent. Within policies set by the security team, the AI Security Engineer for Data is designed to gather the evidence on a flagged risk before remediating it on its own.

The platform is being pitched as a way to bring together work that enterprises typically buy as five separate products: data security posture management, data detection and response, database activity monitoring, data loss prevention and insider risk management.

Coming into its new funding round, Matters.AI has been deployed at more than 50 organizations. Customers include major financial institutions, brokerage and asset management firms, large retailers and digital media and entertainment platforms, the company says.

“Enterprises want to move fast with AI, but no one can trust an agent with data they cannot follow,” Harsh Sahu, co-founder and chief technology officer of Matters.AI, said in the company’s announcement. According to Sahu, the platform works across petabytes of data and billions of access events a day.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Keshava Murthy argued that security teams do not need “another tool telling them something might be wrong,” adding that they instead need a system that can investigate a problem and take action.

Tanglin Venture Partners Pte. Ltd. led the pre-Series A round, with IIFL Fintech Fund, Piper Serica’s Bharat Tech Fund, Foster Ventures and Tetration Ventures also participating. Existing investors Kalaari Capital and Endiya Partners also invested in the round. The pair co-led a $4.75 million seed round announced in October 2025, when Matters.AI also disclosed an earlier $1.5 million pre-seed round led by Better Capital and Carya Venture Partners.

Sankalp Gupta, managing partner at Tanglin Venture Partners, said that rather than “adding another layer of alerts, the team is rethinking how enterprise data security operates.”

Research and development in data lineage, autonomous investigation, endpoint and browser intelligence and the prevention of sensitive data misuse by AI agents will be the focus of the money raised. Including the new funding, Matters.AI has raised $18.25 million to date.

#5278. Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm

Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the company wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”

Amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled plans to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6

City leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company said it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

#5277. Georgia builders give affordable housing an essential new identity

Georgia residential developers and builders are rebranding affordable housing as essential homes, aimed at workers like teachers and first responders. The effort is linked to policy priorities such as permit review accountability under SB 447 and changes to final plat and bonding.  AI Summary

Put an affordable housing project on a planning commission agenda, and the neighborhood naysayers come out of the woodwork to fight.

They argue it will destroy the neighborhood’s character. Labeling the development as workforce housing doesn’t help much.

What’s in a name? An affordable home – or neighborhood – by any other name is still affordable, no? Still, companies rebrand when the current brand is struggling. And Georgia homebuilders and land developers are taking a crack at giving “affordable housing” a brand makeover, one that’s less stigma and more economic and social fabric dynamism.

The Georgia Residential Land Development Council and the Home Builders Association teamed up to dub affordable housing “essential homes.” They are pairing it with a tagline: “Homes for the people who keep Georgia working.”

But defining essential homes as housing that workers can afford near where they work could be applied broadly as lawmakers from the federal to local levels wrestle with how to make housing more affordable.

“It’s a reality nationally that the buying power of the average American is not considered in land use and zoning policies,” Jay Knight, GRLDC’s chairman, told HousingWire TBD. “Essential homes for essential people intends to move the conversation from sticks and bricks allowed to the important people being prohibited.”

The definition names no home size or price point. It asks whether the people who work in a community can afford to live there. Teachers, firefighters, nurses, first responders, healthcare workers and skilled tradespeople are among the livelihoods the term “essential” captures best. They also include younger Georgians hoping to buy a first home.

Austin Hackney, HBAG’s executive vice president, said in a statement that the term puts a human face on the affordability debate. He said that when workers can’t find homes within reach of their income, the effects reach employers, schools and local businesses.

The rebrand comes with a policy push. The groups say zoning restrictions, long permit reviews, infrastructure requirements and delayed final plat approvals add substantial costs that end up in home prices.

GRLDC helped advance Senate Bill 447, which took effect July 1. The law sets timelines and accountability for Georgia’s land disturbance permit reviews. The council’s next target is final plat and bond reform. It wants reasonable approval timelines, standardized bonding requirements, and an end to delays that keep completed developments from moving forward.

The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development considers housing affordable when occupants pays no more than 30% of gross income on housing costs. Programs add other definitions, often tied to area median income. Affordable housing typically targets households at 60% of the area median income or less, while workforce housing covers roughly 60% to 120%.

Workforce housing, however, isn’t explicitly defined in federal law or regulation, according to a March 2026 Congressional Research Service analysis. But the term is used to avoid saying a housing development is affordable housing.

Opposition often centers on neighborhood character. Researchers also find residents may fear newcomers’ socioeconomic status more than the buildings themselves. Property values are another common worry, though research cited by the Florida Housing Coalition found almost no negative effect on neighboring market-rate homes.

Knight said the definition problem became clear at a speaking engagement. He asked a room of roughly 40 people to define affordable housing. One woman said Section 8. Someone else said anything under $400,000. A person from the Northeast thought it meant rent control.

Knight said that convinced him people weren’t talking about the same thing, which made the conversation unproductive. His business partner suggested essential homes. Knight said the organizations liked it immediately.

Terms such as affordable homes, starter homes, first-time buyer or workforce housing arrive with a definition already attached. Knight said “essential homes” encourages people to ask what it means, which gives the groups a chance to set the definition themselves.

The rationale behind the rebranding is that if local governments can dictate what can be built, the standard shouldn’t exceed what their own employees can buy. Knight said the average municipal employee earns about $60,000 to $62,000 a year in Georgia. That means they can afford about a $225,000 home.

In most U.S. markets today, that would buy roughly 1,100 square feet on a 35-foot detached lot, with no garage and no homeowners association, he said. He added that would put the price at about three and a half times annual income, close to the ratio GIs returning from World War II paid in the late 1940s and 1950s.

Knight said zoning conditions have pushed home prices to a much higher ratio. High-cost areas like California, New York and Florida are prime examples. In Silicon Valley, the median home price is 11.4 times median household income, according to an annual report from Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. The Miami metro’s ratio is 7.6.

High prices relative to income are a major reason the median first-time homebuyer is now 40. It’s an all-time high, according to the National Association of Realtors. Such a disparity is why California and Florida have been at the forefront of housing reforms.

The Georgia campaign will put faces to the term: a police officer, a teacher, a nurse and a forklift operator. Knight said it will portray the kinds of workers that municipalities court with industry.

Knight, who sits on an advisory council for the National Association of Home Builders, said he has shared the term with the executive director of the Houston Home Builders Association. He said Houston is now discussing it, since builders nationwide are having the same conversations.

“Who can be against essential housing?” Knight said.

#5276. For Asia-Pacific, Strategic Clarity Is the Key to Value

SINGAPORE, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Only 20% of employees in Asia Pacific have strong strategic clarity about AI, according to a new report from Boston Consulting Group (BCG). Among regular AI users in APAC, strong strategic clarity lifts the number of employees reporting measurable business impact by 22 percentage points, versus 4 percentage points for access to AI tools.

Employees with strong strategic clarity know that AI is a priority, understand the strategy and their role in it, and have clear guidance on what to do with the time AI saves. Communication also shapes trust. Where employees say leadership communicates very clearly about AI, 61% fully trust leadership, compared with 3% where communication is not clear.

These are among the findings of For Asia-Pacific, Strategic Clarity Is the Key to Value, BCG's second annual APAC AI at Work report, based on a survey of 6,349 employees in Australia, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea, and Thailand. Respondents in Australia, India, and Japan were surveyed for the global AI at Work 2026 study of 11,749 employees, published in June, and the rest in September and October.

AI use is now near-universal across Asia Pacific. Eighty-five percent of employees use it regularly, up from 78% in 2025 and in line with 84% globally. Japan saw the sharpest increase over the past year, from 51% to 79%, while India leads the region at 96%.

Far fewer employees use AI deeply. Only 26% use it regularly and for at least half of their daily tasks. Those employees save an average of 14.3 hours a week, compared with 6.2 hours for people who use AI less than a few times a week.

Many companies are going beyond deploying AI tools. Sixty-nine percent of APAC employees say their organization uses AI to reshape end-to-end work, compared with 57% globally, while 45% say it is used to invent new business models. At companies that reshape or invent with AI, 60% of employees report measurable business impact, compared with 43% at companies that only deploy AI tools.

"Getting AI into employees' hands was the easy part, and Asia Pacific has largely done it," said Jeff Walters, managing director and senior partner at BCG and a coauthor of the report. "The measurable impact comes from what happens next, when companies rebuild how work gets done around AI."

The report also finds a "joy paradox," with work becoming both more demanding and more enjoyable. Among employees with strong strategic clarity, 76% enjoy their work more and 47% report a higher cognitive load, versus 30% and 21% with no clarity. Only 7% of them are anxious about AI, against 19% without clarity.

"Each market in Asia Pacific needs its own playbook, but three priorities hold everywhere," said Romain de Laubier, Asia-Pacific regional chair at BCG X and a coauthor of the report. "Make strategic clarity the number one priority, measure the value AI creates rather than how much it is used, and put the guardrails in place to use it responsibly."

#5275. RBC Signals brings in $10M investment to expand strategic frontiers for satellite services

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 6:33 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 6:33 pm

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has announced a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the company’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals announced a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

The newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, said today in a news release.

“By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith said. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.
