#5258. Your Customers Just Got an AI Agent. Is Your Business Ready to Talk to Them?

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Personal AI agents are now customers. Here’s how businesses can prepare.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Right now, companies are interacting with customers who are not giving up, losing their patience after being put on hold or missing what’s in the fine print of the business’s policies. That’s because these customers aren’t humans. They’re personal AI agents acting on behalf of humans.

Meta’s Muse and xAI’s Grok Bot are the two getting the most attention right now. Muse skyrocketed up to number one in the App Store, and Meta’s stock jumped double digits in the same week. Financial markets have been trying to price what these personal agents mean for retail, travel and banking. Massive corporations are already reacting, with Amazon blocking Muse outright and Shopify electing to build Muse its own checkout lane instead.

There’s a lot of noise right now about what these personal AI agents should and will be allowed to do. The dust has clearly not settled, and some very important questions hang in the air. But make no mistake: This will not be a passing trend or a footnote in the broader story of AI innovation. This is a massive shift in how businesses interact with customers, and the companies that start getting ready for it now are the ones who will be prepared when it arrives at their front door.

From the consumer’s perspective, a personal agent fights the battles they don’t want to, and does so more rigorously than they ever could.

Someone’s flight gets cancelled, and their personal agent can argue with the airline until it gets a credit. Someone points it at subscription services and gets every one to offer a discounted rate. I’ve seen dozens of these examples pile up on social media over the past few weeks, and the pattern is always the same. A task a person would normally decide was not worth the trouble is now getting done anyway, because an agent has no concept of trouble.

We used to think about bots talking to bots like something that will happen “someday.” It’s happening now. For consumers who don’t want to solve problems through sheer persistence and patience, this is an exciting development. For businesses that have built their customer service programs around interacting with humans, this is a challenge to solve, fast.

The simple response to this innovation sounds like: “We need our policies to be accurate, because AI will be better at calling us out on them than a human customer.” It goes deeper than that. Every refund policy and guarantee clause has fine print and phrases that are ever so slightly open to interpretation. Personal AI agents can read these policies and find where they bend in ways a human never could.

And they’ll do this at scale. One customer raising a question and finding a loophole is a cost of doing business. Thousands of agents doing the same thing can overwhelm a business, both financially and operationally.

That kind of volume does not behave like a normal surge in customer support demand. It behaves more like a denial-of-service attack. Nobody debates whether each individual request is legitimate; the volume itself is the problem. The response has to be infrastructural: detecting, filtering, a real system for deciding what gets through. “We will deal with it when it happens” is not a strategy at this scale.

Retail and travel may seem like the industries most vulnerable to risk, but any business with documented policies faces the same exposure. Insurance, financial services, healthcare — wherever a company has put a promise or statement of intent in writing, an agent can find it and act on it.

AI has already carved out a massive role in how businesses interact with customers. Now it’s showing up on the other side of the conversation. Nobody has every single answer for how to prepare for this new reality, us included. But there are foundational moves worth making now, rather than waiting for the rest of the industry to decide what to do.

First, there’s the question of identity. Most businesses have no reliable way to know whether they are talking to a customer, a customer’s authorized agent or something pretending to be one. That infrastructure needs to be in place before anything else matters.

Second, you need visibility into what is already happening. You need to be able to see how often an agent is showing up in a support queue, what it’s asking for and how often it’s succeeding.

Then there’s the issue of the policies themselves. A traditional review to ensure accuracy is no longer sufficient. Businesses need to audit their policies, line by line, and stress-test every potential ambiguity that could turn into a vulnerability. Find the gaps before an agent does.

Resist the instinct to default to blocking. Throughout history, we’ve seen what happens to companies that try to close a door that’s going to be kicked down regardless. Search engines that tried to wall off the open web lost to the ones that stayed open, and the same pattern is likely to repeat here. Open does not mean undefended. It means building real verification and governance instead of a blanket “no,” even while the rest of the playbook is still being written.

Big players are picking sides right now, with Amazon blocking personal agents and Shopify building a lane. It’s tempting to treat their moves as a test case, something to monitor from the sidelines until the winds blow in one definitive direction.

That would be a mistake. Sure, the headlines may change in a week; in the case of these specific AI agents and the companies that created them, there may be developments that complicate their rapid surge in the short term. But the shift is happening, and CX organizations can’t be lulled into a reactive posture.

Nobody has built the perfect system for this yet. But the companies spending this period of uncertainty getting their infrastructure ready will be the ones with real footing when the dust settles. Everyone else will still be reading the news, wondering what to do next.

Right now, companies are interacting with customers who are not giving up, losing their patience after being put on hold or missing what’s in the fine print of the business’s policies. That’s because these customers aren’t humans. They’re personal AI agents acting on behalf of humans.

Meta’s Muse and xAI’s Grok Bot are the two getting the most attention right now. Muse skyrocketed up to number one in the App Store, and Meta’s stock jumped double digits in the same week. Financial markets have been trying to price what these personal agents mean for retail, travel and banking. Massive corporations are already reacting, with Amazon blocking Muse outright and Shopify electing to build Muse its own checkout lane instead.

There’s a lot of noise right now about what these personal AI agents should and will be allowed to do. The dust has clearly not settled, and some very important questions hang in the air. But make no mistake: This will not be a passing trend or a footnote in the broader story of AI innovation. This is a massive shift in how businesses interact with customers, and the companies that start getting ready for it now are the ones who will be prepared when it arrives at their front door.

In Ripple news today, XRP is showing signs of a potential rebound in this brutal November, with price bouncing from under $0.9 low to $0.93 as bulls return to the crypto market. Bitcoin and Ethereum have started recovering, but Ripple’s token has yet to catch the same speed and momentum. That could change if XRP manages to defend the $0.90 region.

XRP has fallen by 25% this month as the same correction wiped out much of its recent momentum. Despite the sluggish recovery, XRP is far from an isolated disaster. The crypto market has endured heavy liquidations and risk-off selling, while money rotates toward AI stocks and other opportunities.

The November sell-off has taken XRP well away from its July 2025 peak near $3.65. Yet the decline has also pushed its daily Relative Strength Index below 30, placing the token in oversold territory.

That reading comes as sentiment across crypto has turned deeply pessimistic. Leveraged traders have been forced out of positions, ETF investors have withdrawn capital, and altcoins have struggled to attract fresh liquidity. XRP has been caught in that rotation, rather than facing a sudden deterioration in its own ecosystem. U.S. spot XRP ETFs have recorded roughly $30 million in November outflows, while combined assets have slipped below $1 billion.

Meanwhile, news on Ripple business and the XRP Ledger continues to move forward. RLUSD activity, network development, new lending infrastructure, and ongoing amendment votes are adding to the ecosystem. Those developments haven’t prevented the correction, but they give investors something beyond price action to revisit when risk appetite returns.

XRP is also approaching a potentially attractive zone for longer-term buyers. Prices between $0.70 and $0.90 have become a key area of interest after the token briefly touched the lower end of that range. A sustained recovery in the wider market could make current prices look less intimidating.

XRP’s immediate challenge is to turn its weekend recovery into something more convincing. The token needs to reclaim $0.95 before $1 becomes a realistic short-term target. A clean move above the psychological barrier could open the way toward $1.05 and $1.10 as traders look for momentum to return.

The downside remains clear. Another break below $0.90 might send XRP back toward $0.86, where buyers stepped in during the latest flush. That level is important because another rejection could undermine the recovery attempt and extend the correction.

But XRP doesn’t need a spectacular catalyst to bounce. The market has already priced in a painful November, momentum is stretched, and sentiment is heavily tilted toward caution. If Bitcoin stabilizes and ETF outflows slow, XRP could have room for a sharp recovery.

For now, $0.90 is the level to watch. Holding it could give XRP the breathing room it needs to reclaim $1 and put November’s sell-off behind it.

#5256. Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am

In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley said that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals issue ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal update at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”

Last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says his company’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

It will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t update for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

There’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

#5255. DeSantis says a Florida city misread his anti-DEI law. Now a nonprofit needs $130,000 to save its St. Patrick’s Day parade

Delray Beach, Florida, had set aside about $77,000 for its St. Patrick’s Day parade, according to local reports. Now a local nonprofit says it will take $130,000 to run the event without the city, and its fundraiser has raised nearly $2,900.

The city has celebrated St. Patrick’s Day for more than 50 years with a parade of floats and marching bands that draw an average of 42,000 spectators, according to the city’s report for sponsors. But on Nov. 10, Delray Beach announced it’s canceling the 2027 parade along with its Pride event because of a new state law officials argue makes it illegal to celebrate a specific group of people—in this case, the Irish.

“Following a review of the legislation and its requirements, the City has determined that it is legally prohibited from organizing, funding, sponsoring, promoting, or marketing these two events in 2027,” a City of Delray Beach spokesperson told Fortune. “This decision is not budgetary in nature, nor is it the result of a local policy decision. It is a matter of compliance with state law, which applies to municipalities throughout Florida.”

The law is part of Florida’s broader crackdown on DEI—which has included restricting discussions of gender in public schools and ordering the removal of rainbow crosswalks—but its effect on Delray Beach shows how far its reach could extend: a measure targeting DEI is now being interpreted as a reason to cancel a celebration of Irish heritage that predates the DEI political debate. Now, the governor who signed it says Delray Beach has it wrong.

“Delray Beach is engaging in ‘malicious compliance,’” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis posted on X. “What they are doing is not mandated by Florida law. It’s just an attempt to make a political point.”

Signed by DeSantis in April, the bill prohibits local governments from organizing or promoting “training, programming, or activities designed or implemented with reference to race, color, sex, ethnicity, gender identity, or sexual orientation,” and it will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027. St. Patrick’s Day isn’t among the observances the law exempts.

“St. Patrick’s Day is not a federal holiday and, in this context, does not qualify for an applicable exemption,” the Delray Beach spokesperson said. “As a result, the annual parade is subject to the law’s restrictions.”

But the bill’s sponsor says that’s not what the bill was intended to do. “When the bill was on the Senate floor, the specific question was asked related to whether St. Patricks [sic] Day observances would be prohibited,” State Sen. Clay Yarborough wrote on X. “The answer was and still is no.”

Despite the political criticism, some local officials are open to other ways to make the parade happen. Republican Mayor Tom Carney told NPR, “It’s engrained in the DNA of Delray” and he would be open to private sponsors taking over to host the festivities. City Manager Terrence R. Moore is also open to this, per the Delray Beach spokesperson. She said the city has received an application from Delray Beach-based events company Festival Management Group to host the parade, but it’s still in the “very early stages of the city’s special events process.” Festival Management Group did not respond to Fortune’s requests for comment.

Going private will cost more than the city spent. Delray Beach had budgeted $77,000 for the parade, according to local reports. Now a nonprofit is trying to raise nearly twice that. Delray Beach Arts Inc. has applied to the city to produce the 59th Annual St. Patrick’s Day Parade on Saturday, March 13, joining Festival Management Group as a would-be host.

The group puts its projected production budget at approximately $130,000, covering public safety, traffic management, barricades, insurance, permits, entertainment, equipment, staffing, and professional event management. A GoFundMe for the effort had raised $2,885 as of Monday afternoon.

“While the City can no longer legally provide municipal funding or promotional support for these events, the legislation does not prohibit private organizations or individuals from independently sponsoring and organizing them,” the Delray Beach spokesperson said.

The city’s decision comes as Florida cities brace for a property tax cut that is already forcing some to drop events and services, Fortune reported.

The law also reaches private companies. Starting Jan. 1, any business seeking a contract or grant from a Florida city or county must certify that it does not and will not use county or municipal funds in requiring its employees, contractors, volunteers, vendors, or agents to ascribe to, study, or be instructed using materials relating to diversity, equity, and inclusion.

Delray Beach’s decision mirrors a retreat corporate America has been making for two years, as companies cut DEI programs and language under legal and political pressure. The stakes for the city’s officials are steep: under the law, an official who violates it commits misfeasance or malfeasance in office, and residents can sue their city.

Walmart became the largest company to pull back its DEI policies in late 2024, after Ford, Harley-Davidson, Lowe’s and Tractor Supply had already done so. Meta followed in January 2025, terminating its DEI programs, including those involved in hiring, training and choosing suppliers. After Target pulled back its DEI programs in January 2025, a boycott followed, and the company missed analysts’ sales expectations by nearly half a billion dollars, though analysts also blamed problems in its stores, and it seemed to recover foot traffic this past quarter.

#5254. He Retired at 50. At 70, He’s Working 7 Days a Week on His Biggest Idea Yet.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Peter Castleman could have spent retirement playing golf — instead, he built WISEcode, an AI-powered food transparency platform.

If you’re like me, your approach to nutrition mostly involves squinting at a label, not recognizing any of the ingredients, and eating the thing anyway. Peter Castleman decided that wasn’t good enough. After four decades as an investor, including as Chairman and Managing Partner of J.H. Whitney & Co., where he played a role in investments tied to The North Face, Igloo and Herbalife, Peter came out of retirement to become the founder and CEO of WISEcode, an AI-powered food transparency platform that has mapped more than 840,000 products. He’s 70 years old and says he’s never felt more excited about an idea, proving it’s never too late to chase a big idea.

Give us the elevator pitch. What is WISEcode?Basically, we’re trying to solve what I call the food information crisis. We literally don’t know two things: what’s in our food and what it does to us. At WISEcode, we’ve been spending a dozen years or so solving that. We’ve created what we call the Food Genome Project, which is really mapping the entire food system. So we now know exactly what’s in our foods, and we can tell you what it does for you. And that applies to consumers, policymakers, government people, industries, retailers, scientists, everyone. That information didn’t exist, and now it does.

This isn’t the first company you’ve started or been a big part of. Why did you want to become a founder again?Well, I’m 70, okay? When I turned 50, I retired from my firm. I’m healthy. I eat generally well. But when you turn 50, you enter the kill zone for chronic disease, and chronic disease is 90% of our health issues, and 80% of chronic disease is driven by what we choose to do. We actually control most of our health outcomes. So I basically wanted to simply hack what I’m going to eat. I didn’t want to get cognitive issues. I didn’t want to get any late-onset chronic disease. But that hack doesn’t exist. It shocked me. It just doesn’t exist. So this passion became the business purpose of WISEcode, and I said, “Okay, I’m gonna get this information. I’m going to do for me, I’m going to do for every single individual. I’m going to give them Food Truth.” Formally, I’ve probably been doing this for about 12, 13 years. Informally, I’ve been thinking about it for 20 years.

When a business is a personal passion, do you have a process for figuring out whether it will be a passion for other people, too? Or do you just follow your heart?Like many people, I suffer from that latter part, which is letting your emotions get too far into stuff. I’ve always said, “Fall in love with your family and your friends, not your businesses.” It’s hard to do, because you develop passions. I have three tests I generally apply to any kind of activity. The first I call the North Star test: is it very clear that what you’re trying to do resonates with others? Is it going to be an aha moment or a so-what moment to the world? Number two, I call the sandbox test. How big is your sandbox? How big is your addressable market? And how crowded is your sandbox? And then the third one I call the moat test, which is: can you build defensible business assets that prevent people from copying what you do? People will copy you in a second if you’re successful. If I’m not slam-dunk strong on all three tests, I try to stay away. I apply that to WISEcode. I apply it to everything I do. I’m better at it now than I was at 25.

How do you figure out if other people are interested in your idea when you don’t have a big budget?Social media and everything we have today are double-edged swords. But I use SurveyMonkey all the time. You can ask a question and, for not very much money, you can get 500, 1,000 really clear answers that help you evolve. You can do the same thing on social media tools. The tools out there today are so great. It used to be you’d have to hire McKinsey or Bain for a gazillion dollars, and they’d do a six-month study. Now, in a day, you can get better information than they ever gave you.

What do you say to someone in their 50s who thinks, “I always wanted to do my own thing, but it’s too late”?First and foremost, I think you gotta be honest with yourself. Who are you? What do you love doing, and are you good at this? Late in your career, any time, if you don’t have the energy, the drive and the staying power, don’t do it. Because building companies is hard. You’re going to get knocked on your fanny a ton of times. You gotta get back up. You gotta inspire others around you. You gotta keep going when everyone says, “Don’t do it.” You’re gonna run out of money. You’re gonna have your spouse saying, “What the hell are you doing?” But if it’s in your DNA, it’s the greatest thing in the world. Most of my contemporaries are reducing their handicap on the golf course, and I’m spending 10 hours a day, seven days a week on WISEcode, and I love it. I wouldn’t change it for the world, but that’s me. The greatest joy I get, besides my love of my friends and family, is building businesses that actually make a difference, and if that’s in your DNA, do it. I think the only failure in life is not trying.

#5252. ‘Voluntary, revocable’: The fine print behind Anthropic founders’ $112 billion giving pledge

Anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled. Its size depends on a stock that has swung more than $30 a share in its first three sessions.

The Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov. 18, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, raising a record $81.3 billion and valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The stock opened at $111.50 on Nov. 19, closed its first day at $97.17, then fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday.

On Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way. Shares closed down 1.4% at $87.64, about 5.6% above the IPO price.

TechCrunch estimated Thursday that Anthropic’s charitable commitments could be worth about $156 billion at roughly $95 a share, where the stock traded early in its debut. The figure combines the company’s Public Benefit Fund, employees’ pledged shares and Anthropic’s match on those pledges.

Because all three are paid in stock, the total moves with the share price. At Monday’s close, the same math yields about $144 billion, down $12 billion from Thursday. At the $83 IPO price, it would be roughly $136 billion.

Even the lower figures are enormous. By TechCrunch’s count, Americans gave $617 billion to charity in all of 2025, so Monday’s value equals nearly a quarter of a year of U.S. giving.

The largest piece is the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a wholly owned LLC the company announced in October. Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows it contributed 846.8 million shares to the fund, 5% of fully diluted shares as of June 30, a stake worth about $74 billion at Monday’s close.

The fund can grow. Anthropic says its board may add another 2% of the company for every 50% increase in value above a set baseline; TechCrunch reported that baseline is the $83 IPO price, which would put the next trigger near $124.50 a share. The company said it will disclose more about the fund’s governance and valuation milestones in the coming months, and it has not announced a distribution timetable.

The second channel is employees. About half of Anthropic’s staff take part in its equity donation program, and the company matches pledged shares 3-for-1 for longer-tenured employees and 1-for-1 for newer ones, according to plan documents filed with the S-1. TechCrunch estimated employees have pledged about $23 billion in stock, which would draw roughly $53 billion in matches at $95 a share.

That money is closer to moving, but not yet. Most holders face a lockup of up to 180 days, which could end sooner after first-quarter 2027 results, and many employees cannot sell or gift most of their shares until next spring, the Associated Press reported. Shares parked in donor-advised funds, which have no annual payout requirement, may take even longer to reach working charities.

The third channel is the least certain. Anthropic’s seven cofounders have pledged to give away 80% of their personal equity, a commitment the AP valued at $112 billion at the IPO price. But the S-1 describes the pledges as “voluntary, revocable expressions” of intent that are not legally binding, and timing, amounts and recipients remain undecided. TechCrunch’s $156 billion estimate excludes them.

The cofounders also face the longest lockup: up to 365 days from the Nov. 18 prospectus, or earlier after third-quarter 2027 results, with a portion of their shares eligible for release around the 180-day mark.

Some money is already committed. Earlier this month, Anthropic pledged $50 million to a donor-advised fund at the San Francisco Foundation for Bay Area nonprofits through 2027. The first $500,000 went to the SF-Marin Food Bank, GLIDE, the Interfaith Winter Shelter and the San Francisco Firefighters Local 798 Toy Program, and a company spokesperson told TechCrunch the gift did not come from the Public Benefit Fund.

Anthropic has also committed $200 million to study and address AI’s effects on the labor market. In June, it pledged $150 million to Claude Corps, a fellowship that places early-career workers at nonprofits to help them use AI.

Separately, Anthropic has given $40 million this year to Public First Action, a bipartisan group that advocates for AI safeguards. That is policy spending, not charity, and Anthropic says it will not use equity held by the Public Benefit Fund for lobbying or political giving.

The next test for the share price comes Dec. 15, when up to 303 million shares can become eligible for sale under the prospectus’s lockup schedule, followed by another 303 million on Jan. 5. For charities, the date that matters more is spring 2027, when employee pledges and the company’s matches can start to move.

Until then, Anthropic’s philanthropic promise is marked to market every trading day. A return to the $115 debut high would lift TechCrunch’s measure to nearly $190 billion; a slide below $83 would take it under $136 billion.

#5251. Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

The new funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the company-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

“The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”

Marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis said the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight company acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders said the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis said.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The company isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders said. A second, larger site using AMD’s new Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The company says it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan said that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a new AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he said.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe plans to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

The $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis said. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis said the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one big customer that could pull out.

Ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”

#5250. With Jensen Huang back as CEO, Nvidia’s SEC probe puts CFO Colette Kress in the spotlight

Following Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, Colette Kress is no longer interim CEO. But as finance chief, a lingering Securities and Exchange Commission investigation could put Kress under scrutiny, raising questions about her future at the AI giant.

The Fortune 500 company announced Monday that Huang had been reinstated as president and chief executive officer and as a member of the board, effective immediately. He had stepped down on Nov. 12 amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman some officials believed was a Chinese spy. The White House told Fortune that “President Trump was totally involved” in Huang getting reinstated, and Trump said the U.S. government did not believe Huang’s return posed any national security risk.

“We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s chief financial officer,” the company announcement said.

While the announcement indicated a return to Nvidia’s previous management structure, with Kress back in the finance chief role she’s held for the past 13 years, that may not be as easy as it appears. For one thing, it’s unclear whether the relationship between Kress and Huang has been damaged by the events of the past two weeks. And with Nvidia facing various investigations, Kress could be in the line of fire, depending on the outcome of the probes.

The SEC is investigating Nvidia’s accounting practices, Reuters reported last week. The Wall Street Journal previously reported the investigation, although its precise focus remains unclear. Nvidia didn’t respond to Fortune’s request for comment. An SEC spokesperson said the agency does not comment on “the existence or nonexistence of a possible investigation.”

An investigation does not necessarily mean wrongdoing has occurred. But the scrutiny could put Nvidia’s financial practices and corporate governance under a brighter spotlight, raising questions about what Kress knew about the company’s financial risks and when.

Kathryn Harrigan, a professor at Columbia Business School, pointed to Kress reportedly raising concerns internally last spring about Nvidia’s financial backing of loans to AI startups buying its chips. Kress questioned how borrowers were selected and how guarantees were valued, according to reports.

Nvidia has helped AI startups secure financing to buy its chips, creating a circular flow of money: The company supports buyers financially, and those buyers spend the money on Nvidia products. That makes it harder to assess underlying demand for its chips without that support, Harrigan said.

“In my book, Ms. Kress is a person who’s aware of the problem, and good luck to her if it’s an SEC investigation,” said Harrigan, a corporate strategy specialist. “When I served on boards, I’ve gone through that, and it’s just endless depositions, and they never tell you whether they’re satisfied or not.”

Harrigan added that Huang “had better brush up on whatever he told Ms. Kress back in the spring when they reportedly started to have a disagreement between them about how they were proceeding.”

During Nvidia’s Nov. 17 earnings call, Kress also signaled caution about financial commitments.

“We are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees,” she said, adding that Nvidia would be “disciplined and selective in our support.”

The way that Nvidia accounted for sales in Singapore has also come under scrutiny. Singapore was one of the company’s five geographic revenue locations until mid-2025, when Nvidia abruptly changed how it recorded revenue and removed Singapore from the list of locations. Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer suspected of evading U.S. chip export controls and the company at which Huang’s paramour was an executive, is based in Singapore.

Shawn Cole, president and cofounder of Cowen Partners Executive Search, said an SEC investigation involving financial oversight generally falls within the CFO’s purview.

“Nvidia’s potential exposure to securities class action litigation, compounded by alleged gaps in its directors and officers liability insurance, raises serious questions about corporate governance, financial oversight, and risk management,” Cole said.

Kress could face scrutiny over what she knew about these exposures, when she knew it, and her role in evaluating, disclosing, and mitigating those risks, he said.

Huang could also potentially have exposure for all of the same issues, of course. But as evidenced by Trump’s intervention in the board’s deliberations, the CEO has an important ally in his corner that Kress may not have.

Research suggests CFOs can face career consequences even when they are not implicated in corporate fraud. In “Fraud Firms’ Non-Implicated CFOs,” published in Contemporary Accounting Research, the authors found that roughly one-third of CFOs in its sample were not implicated in the misconduct, yet these executives experienced higher turnover and poorer subsequent employment prospects than peers at comparable companies—evidence that reputational damage can extend beyond those accused of wrongdoing.

When Nvidia announced Kress’s interim CEO appointment on Nov. 12, she said she was “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.” At the end of the Nov. 17 earnings call, she added: “Our customers and our partners are with us and employees are committed; we’ve got this.”

Kress had not publicly expressed interest in pursuing the permanent CEO position. The board had said it would consider internal and external candidates, but Huang’s reinstatement effectively ended that search.

CFOs are increasingly being appointed CEOs, and Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, played an extensive role in the company’s growth, and has vast finance experience at Cisco, Microsoft, and Texas Instruments.

“I’m not sure Kress wants to be CEO, but it is unlikely she will eventually be CEO of Nvidia,” Cole said. “Her short stint as interim CEO wasn’t long enough to impress.”

If Kress decides on her own to leave Nvidia, Cole said, her next step would most likely be retirement.

“I usually try to steer my students by reminding them that if they take a CFO job, that assumes that they know everything about the finances of the company and how the money gets made,” Harrigan said.

Sheryl Estrada is a senior writer at Fortune, where she covers the corporate finance industry, Wall Street, and corporate leadership. She also authors CFO Daily.
